<ConflictType> — conflicting evidence on safety and suitability of one-day dental implants

Evidence clusters show two opposing positions: several provider/clinic sources (d1, d4, d5, d6, d7, d10) assert one-day implants are safe and effective for appropriate candidates, while a critical clinical perspective (d9) and cautionary procedural commentary (d8, d11) highlight risks, suboptimal outcomes, and constraints that undermine blanket safety claims.

The retrieved set collectively supports a conflicted landscape: promotional and procedural descriptions emphasize immediate function and high success rates for carefully selected patients, whereas clinical cautions emphasize risks of infection, bone loss, implant failure, and the need for staged healing in many cases.

One-day dental implants are described by many providers as safe and effective for carefully selected patients, often citing high success rates and immediate function [d1, d4, d5, d6, d7, d10]. However, critical sources warn that full-mouth one-day implants carry substantial risks and can lead to subpar outcomes, especially when bone quality is poor or infection is present [d9]. Mini implants can be immediately loaded but are often intended as temporary solutions rather than permanent replacements, which limits their long-term safety profile [d8]. Timing and site conditions also matter: immediate implant placement shortly after extraction can be riskier due to insufficient bone healing [d11].

Given these conflicting viewpoints, the safety of one-day implants depends heavily on patient selection, bone health, and procedural planning; blanket assurances of safety are not universally supported by the evidence.
